words.textHint: A community of living things interacting with each other and their environment.
A giant ocean wave caused by an underwater earthquake.
A group of stars that forms a recognizable pattern in the night sky.
All the chemical processes your body uses to turn food into energy.
An egg-laying mammal from Australia with a duck-like bill and a beaver-like tail.
A lizard famous for changing its skin color and moving its eyes independently.
An arctic whale with a long spiral tusk, sometimes called the unicorn of the sea.
The invisible force that pulls objects toward the ground and keeps planets circling the sun.
The force that slows things down when two surfaces rub against each other.
Two or more atoms bonded together, like the tiny units that make up water.
The smallest building block of matter, made of protons, neutrons, and electrons.
Tiny single-celled organisms, some of which can make you sick and some that help you.
A tiny germ that invades living cells to make copies of itself and can spread illness.
The preserved remains or imprint of an ancient plant or animal found in rock.
A huge, slow-moving river of ice that carves valleys over thousands of years.
A massive amount of snow suddenly sliding down a mountainside.
When the moon blocks the sun, or the earth's shadow covers the moon.
A space rock burning up as it streaks through the sky, often called a shooting star.
A large rocky object that circles the sun, mostly found between Mars and Jupiter.
An icy space object that grows a long glowing tail when it passes near the sun.
A gigantic collection of billions of stars held together, like our Milky Way.
A region in space with pull so strong that not even light can escape it.
A lab instrument that magnifies tiny things so you can see cells and germs.
How plants turn sunlight, water, and air into their own food.
A thread-like structure in cells that carries your genes; humans have 46 of them.
The twisted-ladder molecule inside cells that carries all your genetic instructions.
The slow change of living species over millions of years, described by Darwin.
When every last member of a species dies out forever, like the dinosaurs.
An animal that hunts and eats other animals to survive.
Colors or patterns that help an animal blend into its surroundings and hide.
The deep winter sleep some animals take to survive the cold months.
The long seasonal journey animals make, like birds flying south for winter.
When bees or wind carry powder between flowers so plants can make seeds.
The sequence showing who eats whom in nature, from grass all the way up to top hunters.
The natural home where a plant or animal lives, like a desert or a rainforest.
A colorful underwater structure built by tiny sea creatures, home to many fish.
The toxic liquid snakes, spiders, and scorpions inject with a bite or sting.
A long period with little or no rain, when land dries up and crops fail.
Melted rock beneath the earth's surface before it erupts from a volcano.
The slow wearing away of rock and soil by wind, water, or ice.
The gas in the air that you breathe in and your body needs to live.
The gas you breathe out, which plants absorb and which warms the planet.
The layer of gases surrounding a planet, which we call the sky on Earth.
The imaginary line around the middle of the earth, halfway between the poles.
Half of a globe or planet, like the northern or southern half of the earth.
The curved path a planet or satellite follows as it circles around another object.
A large laboratory circling the earth where astronauts live and work for months.
A shot that trains your immune system to fight a disease before you catch it.
When your body overreacts to something harmless like pollen, peanuts, or cats.
The hormone that floods your body during fear or excitement, making your heart race.
Your body's defense network that fights off germs and infections.
An automatic body reaction you can't control, like blinking or a knee jerk.
The dramatic body change some animals go through, like a caterpillar becoming a butterfly.
A cold-blooded animal like a frog that lives both in water and on land.
Describes animals that sleep during the day and are active at night.
An animal that eats only meat, like a lion or a wolf.
An animal that eats only plants, like a cow or a deer.
The world's largest lizard, a giant meat-eater from Indonesian islands.
A large hairy spider that some people keep as an exotic pet.
A South American river fish with razor-sharp teeth that feeds in groups.
The measure of disorder in a system, which always increases according to thermodynamics.
The variety of all living species in an area, from tiny microbes to giant trees.
The huge slabs of the earth's crust whose slow movement causes earthquakes.
A microscopic eight-legged creature, nicknamed the water bear, that can survive in outer space.
The colossal explosion of a dying star that briefly outshines an entire galaxy.
A substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up itself.
The natural glow produced by living creatures like fireflies and deep-sea fish.
A close partnership between two different species where each one benefits the other.
The tiny structures famously called the powerhouse of the cell.
Darwin's idea that the best-adapted individuals survive and pass on their traits.
Relating to the strange physics of particles smaller than atoms, where things can be in two states at once.
Energy traveling as waves or particles, the dangerous kind leaks from nuclear material.
A version of a chemical element with a different number of neutrons, used for dating fossils.
The time needed for a radioactive substance to decay to fifty percent of its original amount.
The mirror-opposite of ordinary particles, which annihilates in a burst of energy on contact with normal stuff.
The invisible substance believed to make up most of the universe's mass.
The point of no return around a black hole, beyond which nothing escapes.
A giant colorful cloud of gas and dust in space where new stars are born.
A world that circles a star other than our sun.
The distance a beam travels through space in twelve months, used to measure the cosmos.
A theoretical shortcut tunnel through space and time, popular in science fiction.
A rapidly spinning dead star that sweeps beams of radio waves across space like a lighthouse.
A single particle of light, the smallest possible packet of electromagnetic energy.
The fourth state of matter, a superheated gas of charged particles found in stars and lightning.
The movement of water through a cell's membrane from a weaker solution to a stronger one.
A protein in your body that speeds up chemical reactions, like breaking down food.
A chemical messenger your glands release into the blood to control growth, mood, and more.
A brain cell that sends electrical signals, letting you think, feel, and move.
A Y-shaped protein your blood makes to recognize and attack invading germs.
A fake pill with no medicine that can still make patients feel better because they believe in it.
A random change in genetic code that can create new traits in living things.
A genetically identical copy of a living thing, like the famous sheep Dolly.
A blank-slate building block in the body that can develop into many different types of tissue.
Any microorganism that causes disease, such as a harmful germ or fungus.
A drug like penicillin that kills bacterial infections but does nothing against colds.
The visible glowing surface layer of the sun.
The green pigment in leaves that captures sunlight for making food.
Ground in polar regions that stays frozen solid all year round.
The shimmering curtains of colored light that dance in the polar night sky.
A natural hot spring that periodically shoots a column of boiling water into the air.
The instrument scientists use to detect and record earthquakes.
The famous number system used to rate the strength of an earthquake.
A mineral icicle that hangs from the ceiling of a cave.
Sand, mud, and tiny rock particles that settle at the bottom of rivers and lakes.
The total amount of greenhouse gas a person's lifestyle releases into the air.
How gases in the atmosphere trap the sun's heat and warm the planet.
The protective shield of gas high above Earth that blocks harmful ultraviolet rays.
A fast river of wind high in the atmosphere that steers weather systems and speeds up airplanes.
A periodic warming of Pacific Ocean water that disrupts weather around the world.
An instrument that measures air pressure to help predict the weather.
A smiling Mexican salamander that stays aquatic its whole life and can regrow lost limbs.
A deep-sea fish that dangles a glowing lure in front of its huge jaws to attract prey.
A colorful sea creature whose punch is fast enough to boil water and crack aquarium glass.
How bats and dolphins find objects by bouncing sound waves off them.
A chemical scent signal animals release to attract mates or mark trails.
Any animal without a backbone, like insects, worms, and jellyfish.
An animal or plant so important that removing it would cause its whole ecosystem to collapse.
A hunter at the very top of the food chain with no natural enemies, like an orca.
The shallow round lab plate scientists use to grow bacteria and mold.
A lab machine that spins samples at high speed to separate liquids by density.
